newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's Prodi fails to heal rift on Albania.
newsitem.headline: Italy's Prodi fails to heal rift on Albania.

text.p: Italy's Communist Refoundation party confirmed on Monday that it would break ranks with the centre-left government and vote against deployment of an Italian-led multinational security force in Albania.

The decision by the party's leadership appeared to bury Prime Minister Romano Prodi's hopes for unity in his parliamentary majority when the two houses of parliament vote on whether to approve the mission on Tuesday and Wednesday.

Though Prodi is certain of victory because of opposition backing for the force, it will be the first time that his majority has split on a major policy vote in his 11 months of office and has caused severe strains in his uneasy coalition.
"The leadership decided unanimously to confirm our position," party leader Fausto Bertinotti told reporters.
He said the party would also oppose the force if Prodi were to decide to put the issue to a confidence vote, thus raising a real possibility that the government could fall.
Refoundation is not part of the government but ensures its majority in the lower house, where it holds the balance of power.

Prodi hoped to swing the party into line after a statement from U.N. Secretary General Kofi Annan that swift deployment of the force of up to 6,000 troops was essential to getting relief to Albanians and stopping the country's slide into anarchy.

"The soldiers must be able to move under as broad a political umbrella as possible," Prodi told La Repubblica newspaper in an interview. "We can't send our troops to Albania with political parties taking different positions."
Italy has said the force, approved by the U.N. Security Council on March 28 and code named Operation Alba (Sunrise) by Rome, will start arriving in the week starting April 14.
Italy will provide the biggest contingent, some 2,000 to 2,500 troops, in a force from up to eight nations.

"The aim is to be in Albania from April 14 but it could be April 15 or 16. It's a decision now for military men rather than politicians," deputy foreign minister Piero Fassino told Italian reporters at a European Union meeting in the Netherlands.
France said on Monday that its 1,000-strong contingent would start leaving from the Mediterranean port of Toulon on Tuesday with marines bound for the Albanian port of Durres.

But in Tirana, Albanian Foreign Minister Arjan Starova said force planners were still trying to iron out problems over which national contingents would be deployed where. He voiced concern at the pace of movement.
"We'd like a speedy action. We want this force as soon as possible," Starova told Reuters. "But I have no doubt they will come," he said.
The force will be the first multinational mission led by Italy, Albania's closest economic partner since the end of the Cold War after a history that has swung from aggression to aid.
April 7 was the 58th anniversary of an invasion of Albania by Benito Mussolini's Fascist Italy a few month before the start of World War Two in 1939.

Bertinotti's party argues that Italian troops could face unacceptable risks following the fatal sinking last month of an Albanian refugee boat in a collision with an Italian navy corvette in the Adriatic. He says the U.N. should instead muster a peacekeeping force under its own flag.
